children.text: Governance is not a document

Most organizations that say they govern clinical AI mean they have a committee and a policy. Neither catches the failures that actually occur, because the failures are not policy violations. They are models that work — that do exactly what they were built to do — deployed against a question they were never built to answer.

The two cases below are the best-documented examples in the literature. Both involved widely deployed commercial software. Both passed whatever review the deploying organizations applied. Both were found by outside researchers with access to the deploying institution's own data, which is the single most important operational fact in this lesson.
Case one: the cost proxy

In October 2019, Ziad Obermeyer and colleagues published "Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations" in Science. The subject was a commercial population health risk algorithm — Optum's, applied to roughly 200 million people a year nationally — used to identify patients who should be enrolled in high-risk care management. The researchers studied about 50,000 patients at a large academic hospital: roughly 6,000 self-identified Black and roughly 44,000 self-identified White.

The algorithm contained no race variable. It predicted future health care costs and used that prediction as a stand-in for future health need. That single substitution was the defect. Because less is spent caring for Black patients than for White patients with the same conditions — a consequence of unequal access, not of lesser need — the model read lower spending as lower need.

The measured effect was large. Among patients the algorithm flagged as highest risk, Black patients had 26.3% more chronic conditions than White patients at the same risk score. Only 17.7% of patients the algorithm selected for extra care were Black; the researchers calculated that an unbiased algorithm would have selected 46.5%. Working with the vendor to predict health outcomes rather than costs reduced the disparity by 84%.

No clinician chose this. No policy was violated. A label was chosen because it was convenient and available, and the label carried the structure of the disparity into every downstream referral decision.

children.text: Case two: the sepsis model that was never externally validated

The Epic Sepsis Model was deployed at hundreds of US hospitals as a proprietary early-warning tool. In June 2021, Wong and colleagues published an external validation in JAMA Internal Medicine covering 27,697 patients across 38,455 hospitalizations at Michigan Medicine between December 6, 2018 and October 20, 2019.

The model's area under the curve was 0.63, against the 0.76 to 0.83 range cited in the vendor's own documentation. Sensitivity was 33%, specificity 83%, positive predictive value 12%. In plain operational terms: the model alerted on 18% of all hospitalized patients, missed 1,709 sepsis cases — 67% of all sepsis in the cohort — and a clinician would have to work up 109 alerts to detect one case of sepsis earlier than they would have without it.

That is both failure modes in one system. It missed two thirds of the condition it was sold to detect, and the alerts it did generate were numerous and unspecific enough to guarantee alert fatigue among the clinicians receiving them. Epic subsequently released a revised model in 2022, a gradient-boosted tree that addressed several of the methodological criticisms and, importantly, came with a recommendation that hospitals train it on their own data before clinical use — a substantial departure from the one-size-fits-all model that preceded it.
The governance lesson is the one the accompanying JAMA editorial made directly: nothing about this was discoverable from vendor materials. It required an external validation against local data.

children.text: Both of these passed review

Neither case involved a reckless organization. The population health algorithm was a mainstream commercial product used by health systems and payers across the country. The sepsis model shipped inside the dominant EHR and was switched on by hundreds of hospitals. What both deployments lacked was the same thing: an independent look at how the model performed on local patients, stratified by subgroup, against a clinically meaningful outcome. Governance that consists of approving a vendor and reviewing a policy will reproduce both outcomes exactly.
The four-stage lifecycle

Pre-deployment evaluation. Establish regulatory status — is this software as a medical device, and what clearance does it hold? Establish what the model actually predicts, which for risk tools is frequently not what its name implies. Establish training data provenance and whether the training population resembles yours. Demand published performance stratified by race, ethnicity, age, sex and disability. And establish whether it has been validated in a setting comparable to yours rather than only at academic medical centers.

Implementation and training. Decide where the output appears in the clinical workflow and what the clinician is expected to do with it. Train staff on what the tool does not know and how to recognize an unreliable output, not only on how to click it. Document override protocols. And measure baseline performance before go-live, because without a baseline there is nothing to detect drift against.

Active monitoring. Track performance against that baseline on a fixed cadence. Track it separately for priority populations, because an average conceals exactly the differential the Obermeyer case describes. Maintain a route for clinicians to report cases where an output contributed to harm or delay. And watch override rates: a systematically high override rate is clinicians telling you the tool is not trustworthy, in the only channel available to them.

Vendor management. Performance commitments with specific thresholds and actual remedies, not best-efforts language. Advance notice of model updates with the opportunity to re-evaluate before the update is deployed. Contractual disclosure of demographic performance data. And explicit terms on what patient data the vendor collects and whether it is used to train future versions.
Which stage would have caught each failure
Pre-deployment: what does the model actually predict? —
Optum algorithm: would have surfaced that the label was cost, not health → Epic Sepsis Model: would have surfaced that vendor AUC was self-reported and never externally validated
Pre-deployment: stratified performance disclosure —
Would have exposed differential performance by race before go-live → Less decisive — the model's failure was overall discrimination, not subgroup gap
Implementation: baseline measurement —
Would have established referral rates by subgroup to compare against → Would have established the pre-deployment sepsis detection rate the model had to beat
Monitoring: stratified performance tracking —
The primary control — the disparity was visible in the deploying institution's own data → Would have shown a 12% positive predictive value within weeks of go-live
Monitoring: override rate tracking —
Not applicable — the tool made referrals, not point-of-care alerts → 109 alerts per true case would have produced an unmistakable override signal
Drift, and why monitoring cannot be one-time

A validated model is validated against a population and a practice pattern at a point in time. Both move. Coding practice changes, a new service line opens, a payer mix shifts, a referral pattern reorganizes after a hospital closes a unit — and the relationship the model learned degrades without any change to the model itself. This is drift, and it is invisible unless something is watching for it.

Drift is also the reason the local-validation requirement is recurring rather than a gate passed once. Epic's own revised guidance — train the model on your hospital's data before clinical use — is an acknowledgment that the relationship between inputs and outcomes is local. If it is local, it is also temporal, and a model correct for your population in 2026 is an empirical claim about 2027, not a settled fact.
The regulatory floor is rising

Governance is no longer purely voluntary. The ONC HTI-1 final rule created a certification criterion for decision support interventions that took effect January 1, 2025. Certified health IT must support 13 source attributes for evidence-based interventions and 31 for predictive ones — covering the model's purpose, training data, validation, fairness assessment and maintenance — plus intervention risk management practices for predictive tools the developer supplies as part of its module. It is a transparency regime rather than a performance standard: it does not tell a hospital which models are good, it forces the information a hospital needs to judge that into the open.

The FDA route is separate. Clinical software that diagnoses, treats, mitigates or prevents disease falls under the software as a medical device framework. The FDA had authorized 1,451 AI-enabled medical devices through the end of December 2025, of which 1,104 — 76% — were radiology devices. That concentration matters for rural systems specifically: imaging is both the most mature category of clinical AI and the capability a small hospital with one radiologist covering every modality is least able to staff to volume.

Neither regime relieves the deploying organization of anything. FDA clearance addresses the device as submitted. HTI-1 addresses disclosure. How the tool performs on your patients remains yours to measure.

children.text: The Equity Imperative applied to Technology

The sixth question — is it just? — is not a sixth pillar and not a separate program. It is a test each of the five pillars has to pass on its own terms. For Technology, the Obermeyer case is the clearest statement of what that means in practice, and of why a separate equity workstream would not have helped.

The algorithm had no race variable. An equity review that examined inputs would have found nothing. An equity office reading a model card would have found nothing. The disparity was only visible in stratified output performance against the deploying institution's own patients — which is to say, it was visible only to someone doing ordinary technical validation, correctly, with subgroups broken out.

So the Technology pillar's equity obligation is specific and technical: stratify every performance metric before you report an average, specify demographic completeness in the data layer that feeds the model, and make stratified performance disclosure a contractual term rather than a request. Chapter 4's warning about incomplete race and ethnicity data in commercial claims connects directly here — a model trained or monitored on a dataset that cannot identify subgroups cannot be audited for differential performance, regardless of anyone's intent. The fairness of the model is bounded by the completeness of the substrate.
Stratify before you average

The single highest-yield governance practice is cheap: never accept an aggregate performance number for a clinical AI tool without the same number broken out by race, ethnicity, age, sex, payer and geography. Averages are where differential performance hides, and the Obermeyer finding was recoverable from data the deploying institution already held. If a vendor will not supply stratified performance, that refusal is itself the finding.
Small hospitals cannot do this alone — and should not try

A critical access hospital with one IT staff member cannot run drift monitoring, subgroup audits and adverse event review for every AI tool it deploys. This is the strongest argument for governing clinical AI at the network level: one shared governance function, staffed with analysts no single small hospital could fund, monitoring every deployment across the network under one set of standards. Vermont's clinically integrated network is the intended vehicle, and the same logic applies to any regional network. The alternative is fourteen separate technology decisions, made at fourteen different levels of sophistication, with the weakest setting the network's real floor.
The capability gap nobody budgets for

One more failure mode deserves naming because it is specific to how rural systems buy AI. Ambient documentation tools transcribe clinical conversations, and they are trained predominantly on English. A health system with a growing multilingual population — immigrant communities, seasonal agricultural workers — that deploys a scribe without multilingual capability has introduced a documentation quality gap that falls entirely on the patients least able to absorb it, and has done so through a purchase nobody would have classified as an equity decision.

That is why the Equity Imperative belongs inside the procurement rather than beside it. Multilingual capability documentation, training data provenance, and stratified performance disclosure are evaluation criteria for a technology purchase. Written as grant conditions, they cost nothing. Discovered after deployment, they are a rebuild.

summary: Two documented failures — a population health algorithm that systematically under-referred Black patients, and a sepsis model that missed two thirds of cases while alerting on 18% of admissions — show what ungoverned clinical AI produces. This lesson builds the validation, drift monitoring and bias auditing regime that would have caught both.
